posts.title: <h2>Key Takeaways</h2>  <p>Vietnam's new foreign-trade management framework under <strong>Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP</strong> takes effect on September 5, 2026.</p>  <p>The decree was issued on July 22 and provides detailed implementation rules for Vietnam's Law on Foreign Trade Management.</p>  <p>It replaces the framework previously implemented under Decree No. 69/2018/ND-CP and updates rules affecting prohibited goods, import and export licensing, temporary import and re-export operations and other controlled trade activities.</p>  <p>One provision that international sourcing teams should pay particular attention to is Vietnam's prohibition involving goods produced wholly or partly through forced labour.</p>  <h2>When Does Decree 292 Take Effect?</h2>  <p>The official Vietnamese Government Gazette confirms:</p>  <ul> <li>Decree: 292/2026/ND-CP</li> <li>Issued: July 22, 2026</li> <li>Effective: September 5, 2026</li> <li>Issuing authority: Government of Vietnam</li> </ul>  <p>Companies trading with Vietnam should therefore review affected transactions now rather than waiting for goods to arrive at customs after the effective date.</p>  <h2>What Does the Decree Cover?</h2>  <p>Decree 292 provides implementation rules for several areas of foreign-trade management.</p>  <p>These include:</p>  <ul> <li>Goods prohibited from export or import</li> <li>Goods subject to import or export licensing</li> <li>Conditional trade controls</li> <li>Temporary import and re-export</li> <li>Temporary export and re-import</li> <li>Transit and related foreign-trade procedures</li> <li>Government administration of controlled goods</li> </ul>  <h2>Prohibited Goods Lists Matter</h2>  <p>The decree includes an annex setting out categories of goods prohibited from export or import.</p>  <p>Vietnamese ministries and competent authorities are responsible for publishing detailed product descriptions and HS codes where required.</p>  <p>This makes tariff classification an important first step for compliance.</p>  <p>A commercial description alone may not be sufficient to determine whether a product falls within a controlled category.</p>  <h2>New Attention on Forced-Labour Goods</h2>  <p>One of the most notable provisions is Vietnam's prohibition involving goods mined, produced or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labour.</p>  <p>The measure operates in accordance with relevant international agreements to which Vietnam is a party.</p>  <p>For multinational companies, this means supply-chain labour due diligence is becoming relevant not only when importing into the United States or Europe but also in Southeast Asian trade compliance.</p>  <h2>Why Procurement Teams Should Care</h2>  <p>Forced-labour compliance cannot be solved only by the customs department.</p>  <p>Customs teams normally receive commercial invoices, packing lists and origin information after purchasing decisions have already been made.</p>  <p>But labour-risk information exists further upstream in the supply chain.</p>  <p>Companies may therefore need procurement records capable of identifying:</p>  <ul> <li>Original manufacturer</li> <li>Production facility</li> <li>Raw-material suppliers</li> <li>Country and region of production</li> <li>Subcontractors</li> <li>Available labour-compliance evidence</li> </ul>  <h2>Review Import and Export Licensing</h2>  <p>Businesses dealing in regulated goods should confirm whether the competent Vietnamese ministry requires an import or export licence.</p>  <p>A previous licence workflow should not automatically be assumed to remain correct after the new decree becomes effective.</p>  <p>Importers should verify the current HS classification and applicable ministry before shipment.</p>  <h2>Temporary Import and Re-Export</h2>  <p>Temporary import and re-export transactions are widely used for repair, exhibitions, processing, equipment projects and regional distribution.</p>  <p>These transactions should be reviewed separately from ordinary imports because they can involve specific time limits, licensing requirements and customs controls.</p>  <p>Companies using Vietnam as a regional logistics or processing location should therefore check whether Decree 292 affects their current procedure.</p>  <h2>Do Not Confuse Customs Classification With Trade Permission</h2>  <p>Correctly classifying a product does not automatically mean that it can be freely imported.</p>  <p>Classification answers one question: what tariff item applies?</p>  <p>Trade-control rules answer another: is the product prohibited, licensed, conditional or unrestricted?</p>  <p>Both checks should be completed before shipment.</p>  <h2>What Foreign Exporters Should Ask Their Vietnamese Importer</h2>  <ol> <li>What Vietnamese HS code will be declared?</li> <li>Is the product included in a prohibited or controlled list?</li> <li>Which ministry or authority regulates the product?</li> <li>Is an import licence required before shipment?</li> <li>Have the requirements changed under Decree 292?</li> <li>Does the product involve any forced-labour supply-chain risk?</li> <li>Are additional technical or inspection documents required?</li> </ol>  <h2>What Importers Should Do Before September 5</h2>  <p>Vietnamese importers and multinational companies should consider a targeted review of active SKUs.</p>  <p>Priority should be given to:</p>  <ul> <li>Controlled industrial products</li> <li>Products requiring ministry licences</li> <li>Used or refurbished goods</li> <li>Temporary imports</li> <li>Products with complex upstream supply chains</li> <li>Goods sourced from regions with elevated labour-risk concerns</li> </ul>  <h2>Update Internal Trade-Control Matrices</h2>  <p>Companies operating ERP or global trade management systems often maintain internal matrices linking HS codes to licence requirements.</p>  <p>Those matrices should be reviewed against the new decree and subsequent ministry-level implementation guidance.</p>  <p>An outdated trade-control matrix can result in a shipment being approved internally even though the legal requirement has changed.</p>  <h2>Practical Compliance Checklist</h2>  <ul> <li>Confirm the Vietnamese HS classification.</li> <li>Check the new prohibited-goods lists.</li> <li>Identify the competent Vietnamese ministry.</li> <li>Confirm import or export licence requirements.</li> <li>Review temporary import and re-export procedures.</li> <li>Map suppliers for forced-labour exposure.</li> <li>Retain appropriate supplier and production records.</li> <li>Update customs and trade-compliance matrices.</li> <li>Coordinate with the Vietnamese importer before loading.</li> <li>Monitor ministry-level implementing guidance.</li> </ul>  <h2>Why September 5 Is Not the End of the Review</h2>  <p>The decree establishes the overarching framework, while individual ministries and agencies may publish more detailed product lists, HS codes and procedural guidance.</p>  <p>Businesses should therefore treat September 5 as the beginning of operational implementation rather than the end of the compliance review.</p>  <h2>Conclusion</h2>  <p>Vietnam's Decree 292/2026/ND-CP takes effect on September 5 and updates a major part of the country's foreign-trade management framework.</p>  <p>For most international traders, the practical priority is to confirm whether active products are prohibited, licensed or otherwise controlled under the new structure.</p>  <p>The forced-labour provision also signals a broader trend: <strong>supply-chain traceability and labour due diligence are increasingly becoming import-compliance issues rather than purely ESG matters.</strong></p>  <p>Companies trading with Vietnam should review classification, licensing and supplier data before affected shipments move.</p>  <h2>FAQ</h2>  <h3>When does Vietnam Decree 292/2026/ND-CP take effect?</h3> <p>It takes effect on September 5, 2026.</p>  <h3>When was the decree issued?</h3> <p>The Government of Vietnam issued Decree 292 on July 22, 2026.</p>  <h3>What does Decree 292 regulate?</h3> <p>It provides detailed implementation rules for Vietnam's Law on Foreign Trade Management, including prohibited and controlled goods, licensing and several temporary import-export procedures.</p>  <h3>Does Vietnam prohibit imports connected to forced labour?</h3> <p>The new framework includes a prohibition involving goods mined, produced or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labour, subject to the relevant legal and international-agreement framework.</p>  <h3>Should foreign exporters check Vietnamese HS codes?</h3> <p>Yes. Product classification is essential for determining whether a specific prohibition, licence or other trade-control requirement applies.</p>  <h3>Will additional guidance be issued?</h3> <p>Product-specific requirements and detailed HS classifications may also be published or administered by the competent Vietnamese ministries and agencies, so businesses should continue monitoring implementation guidance.</p>  <h2>Official References</h2>  <ul> <li><a href="https://congbao.chinhphu.vn/van-ban/nghi-dinh-so-292-2026-nd-cp-470149.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Government Gazette of Vietnam — Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP</a></li> <li><a href="https://vanban.chinhphu.vn/?classid=1&amp;docid=218958&amp;pageid=27160&amp;typegroupid=4" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Government of Vietnam — Decree 292/2026/ND-CP</a></li> </ul>  <p><small>This article provides general trade and customs information and does not constitute legal advice. Import and export requirements depend on the exact product classification, transaction, competent ministry and implementing rules in force. Businesses should verify current requirements with Vietnamese authorities, their importer and qualified customs advisers before shipment.</small></p>
